accepted.s:
With reference to India’s nuclear doctrine, consider the following statements:
1. The No First Use policy was announced in 1999.
2. The doctrine was formally adopted in 2003.
3. The Strategic Forces Command was set up in 2003.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: The No First Use policy was announced in 1999, the nuclear doctrine was formally adopted in 2003, and the Strategic Forces Command was also set up in 2003.
accepted.tq: Combine closely related dates and identify the option containing all correct statements.
accepted.sec: Nuclear doctrine 2003 - tenets, NCA, SFC  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which one of the following is NOT a tenet of India’s nuclear doctrine?
o: Massive retaliation to inflict unacceptable damage
Credible minimum deterrence
No First Use of nuclear weapons
Pre-emptive use against every suspected nuclear power
accepted.x: India’s doctrine includes credible minimum deterrence, No First Use and massive retaliation. It does not provide for pre-emptive nuclear use against every suspected nuclear power.
accepted.tq: Find the option that introduces an absolute policy not supported by the doctrine.
accepted.sec: Nuclear doctrine 2003 - tenets, NCA, SFC  [other exams]

accepted.s: Under India’s No First Use policy, nuclear weapons may be used in retaliation against
o: any conventional attack on Indian territory
a nuclear attack on Indian territory or Indian forces
a cyberattack on India’s strategic infrastructure
any military alliance formed against India
accepted.x: India’s No First Use policy permits nuclear weapons only in retaliation against a nuclear attack on Indian territory or Indian forces.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the exact condition attached to a strategic policy from broader military contingencies.
accepted.sec: Nuclear doctrine 2003 - tenets, NCA, SFC  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India’s nuclear doctrine:
1. India has declared that retaliation to a nuclear attack will be massive.
2. India has declared a policy of non-use of nuclear weapons against non-nuclear-weapon states.
3. India keeps the nuclear option open against a major biological or chemical attack.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: All three statements reflect the stated tenets: massive retaliation, non-use against non-nuclear-weapon states and retention of the nuclear option against a major biological or chemical attack.
accepted.tq: Test several policy clauses together, with the inclusive option as the answer.
accepted.sec: Nuclear doctrine 2003 - tenets, NCA, SFC  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Which of the following is associated with India’s continuing nuclear policy?
1. Continued moratorium on nuclear testing
2. Strict export controls
3. Support for disarmament and the Fissile Material Cut-off Treaty
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: India’s nuclear policy includes a continued testing moratorium, strict export controls and support for disarmament and the FMCT.
accepted.tq: Recognise a cluster of related policy commitments rather than an operational doctrine alone.
accepted.sec: Nuclear doctrine 2003 - tenets, NCA, SFC  [other exams]

accepted.s: Who chairs the Political Council of India’s Nuclear Command Authority?
o: The President of India
The Defence Minister
The National Security Adviser
The Prime Minister of India
accepted.x: The Political Council of the Nuclear Command Authority is chaired by the Prime Minister and is the only body authorised to approve the use of nuclear weapons.
accepted.tq: Use the ‘who would do this job?’ method to distinguish the political authority from the advisory authority.
accepted.sec: Nuclear doctrine 2003 - tenets, NCA, SFC  [other exams]

accepted.s: The Strategic Forces Command is best described as
o: a joint research body of DRDO and ISRO
a civilian body regulating nuclear exports
a tri-service command managing and operating India’s nuclear arsenal
a parliamentary committee supervising defence expenditure
accepted.x: The Strategic Forces Command is a tri-service command responsible for managing and operating India’s nuclear arsenal.
accepted.tq: Match the organisation with its precise institutional role.
accepted.sec: Nuclear doctrine 2003 - tenets, NCA, SFC  [other exams]

accepted.s: Agni user trials are conducted under the aegis of which organisation?
o: Nuclear Command Authority’s Political Council
Atomic Energy Regulatory Board
National Disaster Management Authority
Strategic Forces Command
accepted.x: Agni user trials are conducted under the aegis of the Strategic Forces Command.
accepted.tq: Identify the operational agency rather than the policy-making authority.
accepted.sec: Nuclear doctrine 2003 - tenets, NCA, SFC  [other exams]

accepted.s: India has not signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty primarily because it regards the treaty as
o: a treaty limited only to chemical weapons
a treaty that requires membership of the NSG
an agreement that prohibits civilian nuclear energy
discriminatory and reflecting nuclear apartheid
accepted.x: India considers the NPT discriminatory because it creates an unequal division between recognised nuclear-weapon states and other states, a position often described as opposition to nuclear apartheid.
accepted.tq: Link a non-membership status with the stated reason rather than confusing it with another regime.
accepted.sec: Non-proliferation regimes - India's status and reasons  [other exams]

accepted.s: India’s position regarding the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty is that it will not sign the treaty until it is linked to
o: automatic membership of the UN Security Council
a ban on all conventional weapons
time-bound global nuclear disarmament
the abolition of the Nuclear Suppliers Group
accepted.x: India has not signed the CTBT because it seeks a link between the treaty and time-bound global nuclear disarmament; it nevertheless observes a voluntary test moratorium.
accepted.tq: Test the precise reason for non-signature and distinguish it from membership conditions of other regimes.
accepted.sec: Non-proliferation regimes - India's status and reasons  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India and the Nuclear Suppliers Group:
1. India is not a member of the NSG.
2. China has blocked India’s membership of the NSG.
3. India received an NSG waiver in 2008.
4. India follows NSG guidelines.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1, 2 and 3 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
accepted.x: India is not an NSG member, China has opposed its membership, India obtained a waiver in 2008 and follows NSG guidelines.
accepted.tq: Check membership, obstacle, benefit and compliance separately before selecting the coded option.
accepted.sec: Non-proliferation regimes - India's status and reasons  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:
List-I (Regime)
a. Missile Technology Control Regime
b. Wassenaar Arrangement
c. Australia Group
List-II (India’s membership)
i. Member from January 2018
ii. Member from 2016
iii. Member from December 2017

Codes:
o: a–ii, b–iii, c–i
a–iii, b–i, c–ii
a–i, b–ii, c–iii
a–ii, b–i, c–iii
accepted.x: India joined the MTCR in 2016, the Wassenaar Arrangement in December 2017 and the Australia Group in January 2018.
accepted.tq: Start from the sure date-membership pair and eliminate codes with a misplaced regime.
accepted.sec: Non-proliferation regimes - India's status and reasons  [other exams]

accepted.s: India follows non-proliferation and export-control guidelines primarily through
o: the Official Secrets Act and the GST Council
the Environment Protection Act and the Census Act
the WMD Act and the SCOMET list
the Atomic Energy Act and the Finance Commission alone
accepted.x: India implements relevant export-control commitments through the Weapons of Mass Destruction Act and the SCOMET list.
accepted.tq: Identify the correct legal and administrative instruments instead of a neighbouring statutory framework.
accepted.sec: Non-proliferation regimes - India's status and reasons  [other exams]

accepted.s: India supports a universal and verifiable Fissile Material Cut-off Treaty provided that it
o: does not cap India’s existing stockpile
caps India’s existing stockpile immediately
permits unlimited nuclear testing
applies only to non-nuclear-weapon states
accepted.x: India supports a universal and verifiable FMCT, but its position is that the treaty should not cap its existing stockpile.
accepted.tq: Focus on the qualification attached to India’s support for an international treaty.
accepted.sec: Non-proliferation regimes - India's status and reasons  [other exams]

accepted.s: Why do India’s 700 MW Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors not require Nuclear Suppliers Group clearance for their domestic uranium requirement?
o: They use domestic uranium.
They do not require any nuclear fuel.
They use imported enriched uranium only.
They are operated by the NSG Secretariat.
accepted.x: India’s 700 MW PHWRs use domestic uranium, and therefore their fuel requirement does not depend on NSG clearance.
accepted.tq: Apply the stated fuel-source relationship to determine the regulatory consequence.
accepted.sec: Non-proliferation regimes - India's status and reasons  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the three legs of India’s nuclear triad?
o: Cruise missiles, artillery guns and nuclear reactors
Aircraft carriers, attack helicopters and space launch vehicles
Tanks, submarines and unmanned aerial vehicles
Land-based missiles, nuclear-capable aircraft and submarine-launched ballistic missiles
accepted.x: India’s nuclear triad consists of land-based missile systems, air-delivered nuclear weapons and sea-based submarine-launched ballistic missiles.
accepted.tq: Recognise the three-domain structure instead of selecting individual weapons or platforms.
accepted.sec: Nuclear triad - land, air and sea platforms

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the land leg of India’s nuclear triad:
1. It includes the Prithvi series.
2. It includes the Agni series.
3. The missiles may be canisterised and road- or rail-mobile.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: The land leg includes the Prithvi and Agni series, including canisterised systems with road and rail mobility.
accepted.tq: Test platform names together with their mobility characteristics.
accepted.sec: Nuclear triad - land, air and sea platforms

accepted.s: Which pair of aircraft is associated with the air leg of India’s nuclear triad?
o: Jaguar and Mirage 2000
Su-30MKI and Apache
Tejas and C-17 Globemaster
Rafale and MiG-21 only
accepted.x: The air leg is represented by Jaguar and Mirage 2000 aircraft carrying free-fall nuclear bombs.
accepted.tq: Use platform-pair recognition and avoid substituting other aircraft in the Indian fleet.
accepted.sec: Nuclear triad - land, air and sea platforms

accepted.s: The sea leg of India’s nuclear triad is associated with
o: Prithvi and Agni missiles carried by destroyers
Dhanush missiles carried only by submarines
K-15 and K-4 SLBMs carried by Arihant-class SSBNs
Jaguar aircraft operating from aircraft carriers
accepted.x: The sea leg comprises K-15 and K-4 submarine-launched ballistic missiles deployed from Arihant-class SSBNs.
accepted.tq: Match the missile type with its correct launch platform.
accepted.sec: Nuclear triad - land, air and sea platforms

accepted.s: Which of the following statements about Dhanush is correct?
o: It is a free-fall nuclear bomb delivered by Mirage 2000.
It is an SLBM carried by Arihant-class SSBNs.
It was fired from ships including INS Subhadra and INS Rajput.
It is an intercontinental ballistic missile launched from rail platforms.
accepted.x: Dhanush was fired from ships, including INS Subhadra and INS Rajput; it is distinct from the K-15 and K-4 SLBMs deployed on SSBNs.
accepted.tq: Separate an earlier ship-launched system from submarine-launched ballistic missiles.
accepted.sec: Nuclear triad - land, air and sea platforms

accepted.s: Why are SSBNs regarded as the most survivable leg of the nuclear triad?
o: They eliminate the need for land-based deterrence.
They remain permanently visible to adversaries.
They carry only conventional weapons.
Their concealment supports a guaranteed second-strike capability.
accepted.x: SSBNs are difficult to detect and destroy, thereby supporting a reliable second-strike capability that underpins India’s No First Use posture.
accepted.tq: Connect survivability with the strategic purpose of assured retaliation.
accepted.sec: Nuclear triad - land, air and sea platforms

accepted.s: The next strategic step associated with India’s SSBN-based deterrence is
o: ending the No First Use policy
continuous at-sea deterrence
replacement of all missiles by free-fall bombs
complete withdrawal from submarine operations
accepted.x: Continuous at-sea deterrence is identified as the next step in strengthening India’s SSBN-based nuclear deterrence.
accepted.tq: Identify the policy objective that follows from the capability already described.
accepted.sec: Nuclear triad - land, air and sea platforms

accepted.s: According to the SIPRI count cited for June 2026, how many Indian warheads were described as operationally deployed?
accepted.x: SIPRI counted 12 Indian warheads as operationally deployed in the cited June 2026 assessment, linked to SSBN deterrence patrols and canisterised Agni systems.
accepted.tq: Read the exact quantitative figure and distinguish it from nearby numerical distractors.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: The operational deployment of Indian warheads cited in the June 2026 assessment was linked particularly to
o: Dhanush missiles mounted exclusively on aircraft carriers
only free-fall bombs carried by Jaguar aircraft
SSBN deterrence patrols and canisterised Agni missiles
civilian nuclear reactors and space launch vehicles
accepted.x: The cited deployment was linked to SSBN deterrence patrols and canisterised Agni missiles.
accepted.tq: Match a current quantitative assessment with the two capabilities associated with it.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: INS Aridhaman was commissioned in
o: April 2026
April 2025
August 2026
April 2024
accepted.x: INS Aridhaman was commissioned in April 2026.
accepted.tq: Distinguish closely spaced years and months in a current-affairs fact.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly describes the Agni-4 user trial of 6 August 2026?
o: A 4,000 km, two-stage, solid-fuelled and road-mobile missile trial
A submarine-launched missile trial with a range of 12,000 km
A 700 km, single-stage, liquid-fuelled and rail-fixed missile trial
An air-launched cruise missile trial conducted from a Mirage 2000
accepted.x: The Agni-4 user trial on 6 August 2026 involved a 4,000 km-range, two-stage solid-fuel missile that is road-mobile.
accepted.tq: Check range, staging, propulsion and mobility together to reject mixed-platform descriptions.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the United States nuclear triad?
o: Minuteman III ICBMs, strategic bombers and Ohio/Columbia-class SSBNs
Tomahawk missiles, aircraft carriers and attack submarines
Trident submarines, Agni missiles and Mirage 2000 aircraft
Prithvi missiles, Jaguar aircraft and Arihant-class SSBNs
accepted.x: The US triad consists of Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missiles, strategic bombers and Ohio/Columbia-class SSBNs.
accepted.tq: Match a country-specific triad with all three of its stated components.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: India is described as having a fully operational nuclear triad along with which of the following countries?
o: France, the United Kingdom and Pakistan
Japan, Germany and Australia
The United States, Russia and China
Israel, North Korea and Iran
accepted.x: India is described as having a fully operational triad alongside the United States, Russia and China.
accepted.tq: Use the membership comparison rather than selecting other nuclear-capable states.
accepted.sec: Universal angles
